Modern · The Seoul Table

Yangnyeom Fried Chicken

Double-fried chicken meets a gochujang glaze, with the crunch kept front and center.

Korean · Medium · Serves 4

Jump to recipe ↓

Behind the dish

Lane: modern — the double-fry and the toss, the paste's most famous delivery system. Korean fried chicken's argument with the American original is thinness of crust and the sauce: a shattering, thin glass crust from a double fry, and — in the yangnyeom register — a gochujang glaze tossed at the last second, lacquering every crevice without ever sogging the crunch. This is the paste's biggest stage and the site's technique centerpiece: the brine, the starch dredge, the two-stage fry, and the fifteen-second toss. Get these four right and the chicken is the best thing at any table it joins. Heat dial: 3, adjustable at the glaze.

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • Brine the chicken 2 hours — salt, sugar, garlic, and ginger doing quiet work while the oil sleeps. The brined bird fries juicier and seasons deeper than any post-fry sprinkle manages.
  • Drain, dry, and dredge twice-thin: the chicken patted bone-dry, then dredged in the starch mixture in a bag — shaken, not buried. Knock the excess off hard; the coating should be a whisper, a frost of starch, not a batter. Thin is the entire Korean crust argument.
  • The glaze built before the fry — oil, garlic, and gochujang fried together 45 seconds (the bloom, again, the lane's first law), then honey, soy, mirin, and gochugaru stirred in off the heat to a thick lacquer, parked beside the fry station with a wide bowl for the toss.

Let’s make it.

  1. 01
    First fry — cook through: oil at 170 °C (a starch-dusted cube sizzles steadily, not violently), the chicken in uncrowded batches, 6–8 minutes to cooked-through and pale-gold. Drain on a rack. Checkpoint — the first-fry crust is dry, matte, and the meat cooked (a drumette's joint end shows clear juices); this stage sets the crust's architecture and renders the skin's water out from under it.
  2. 02
    Second fry — the shatter: oil up to 190 °C, the same pieces returned for 90 seconds to 2 minutes, until the crust goes deep gold and audibly crackles when two pieces touch. Checkpoint — the crust's test: tap a piece against the rack's edge — it should sound and crack like thin glass. The double fry's physics: the first stage's steam-puffed starch layer sets, and the second's higher heat blasts the residual moisture out of it, leaving the honeycomb of crackle. This is not repetition; it is construction.
  3. 03
    The fifteen-second toss — the sauce's law. The hot chicken into the wide bowl, the warm glaze over, and tossed with two spatulas for ten to fifteen seconds — every surface lacquered, the bowl scraped, service immediate. Checkpoint — the eating test, thirty seconds after the toss: the crust still shatters under the glaze (the toss's brevity is what preserves it — the glaze coats the outside of the crunch, it does not get time to soak in), the sauce's sweet-heat arriving with the crunch, the brined meat juicy underneath. A yangnyeom that has sat five minutes is still good; a yangnyeom eaten in the first minute is the dish this record exists for. Chef’s Note — on oil temperature without a thermometer, the two-stage fry is the one place this site insists you buy the tool — the 170/190 °C split is the dish's physics, and the cube-test guesswork that carries a stir-fry does not carry a double fry. An instant-read probe or a clip-on candy thermometer costs less than one batch of wasted chicken and ends the guessing forever.

Doneness & Quality Checkpoints

  • The brine: 2 hours, drained bone-dry before the dredge.
  • The dredge: starch-frost thin, excess knocked off hard.
  • The fry: 170 °C cook-through, 190 °C shatter, the crust cracked like glass.
  • The toss: fifteen seconds, warm glaze, immediate service.

Finish & Plate

Piled high and lacquered on a platter with pickled radish cubes (the traditional coolant — sweet-sour against the glaze's heat) and cold beer or the sikhye register beside. Napkins beyond reason; the dish demands them.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Crust soggy within minutesGlaze tossed too long or chicken damp at the fryThe 15-second toss; bone-dry before dredging
Crust thick and breadyOver-dredgedA whisper of starch; knock the excess off
Greasy crustOil dropped below 170 °C under a big batchSmaller batches; thermometer's watch
Glaze slid offCold glaze on hot chickenThe glaze warm, the toss immediate
Heat overwhelmingJar ran hot plus gochugaruSkip the gochugaru; more honey

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • The brined, dredged chicken holds 1 day refrigerated before frying. The fried-undressed pieces re-crisp at 190 °C for 60 seconds the next day — then toss fresh. Dressed yangnyeom keeps nothing, by design.
  • Variations: the undressed half with the cho-gochujang dip (#13's second bowl); soy-garlic (the chicken-house's other classic — the glaze's gochujang replaced by soy, butter, and a mountain of sliced garlic); the boneless-strip build for the lunchbox and the buns.
